article.overview: A visible and infrared spectrometer records how sunlight reflected from a surface is split into its colours, from visible light into the near-infrared and, in some instruments, the shortwave infrared. The result is a reflectance spectrum: a curve of brightness against wavelength. Minerals, glasses and hydrated materials absorb light at particular wavelengths, so the shape of the curve is a fingerprint of composition. The class is defined by its wavelength coverage and measurement style (a spectrum of a point or small footprint), not by one design. In scope: spectrometers covering roughly 0.4-2.6 micrometres (as stated by the sources reviewed) that deliver spectra of a point, small footprint or rover-mounted field of view; two lunar examples are covered, the Visible and Near-Infrared Imaging Spectrometer (VNIS) on China's Chang'e-3 and Chang'e-4 rovers, and the Spectral Profiler (SP) on the SELENE (Kaguya) orbiter. Out of scope and cross-referenced: imaging spectrometers that build a spectrum for every pixel over a mapped area from orbit (payload 035, Hyperspectral imager: M3, IIRS, HVM3); multi-band cameras such as the Kaguya Multiband Imager (payload 034, Multispectral imager); near-infrared and shortwave-infrared cameras (payloads 040 and 041); near-infrared-only spectrometers (payload 061); and Raman, LIBS, X-ray, Mossbauer, thermal-emission and ultraviolet spectrometers (payloads 063, 060, 054-055, 064, 076 and 077). Boundary note: payload 041 describes the VNIS shortwave-infrared channel as a single-point spectrometer and refers VNIS to payload 035; this article takes VNIS as its primary home, and the catalogue owner should reconcile the pointers.
article.description: A visible and infrared spectrometer is typically a small optical instrument with collecting optics, a dispersing element that separates light by wavelength, and a detector that records intensity at each wavelength. Two dispersing approaches appear in the lunar examples. Diffraction grating (SELENE Spectral Profiler): the JAXA instrument page states that SP uses two gratings to separate reflected light into 296 wavelengths [6]. Acousto-optic tunable filter (AOTF) (Chang'e-3 and Chang'e-4 VNIS): an AOTF selects narrow bands electronically using an acoustic wave in a crystal; a search summary of the Chang'e-3 VNIS paper describes non-collinear AOTFs as the dispersive elements [1]. The primary paper full text was not retrieved in this run, so this is taken from a secondary summary. Both examples observe reflected sunlight and need a sunlit target. The VNIS includes an in-situ calibration function, and the search summary also mentions a calibration unit with a dust-proofing function [1].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The purpose of a visible and infrared spectrometer is to determine which minerals, glasses and hydrated or altered materials are present at the measured spot. Mineral identification: pyroxene and olivine, the main silicate minerals in mare basalts and mantle-derived rocks, have absorption features in this range (general mineral-spectroscopy knowledge; no specific source was cited for this statement in this run). The 2019 Nature paper on the Chang'e-4 VNIS reports far-side spectra interpreted as low-calcium pyroxene and olivine [2]; this summary is taken from search metadata and the full text was not retrieved in this run. Rock and soil comparison: repeated spectra of different rocks, soils and dusty surfaces can be compared along a rover traverse or across an orbital dataset; a 2020 Remote Sensing paper reports 96 in-situ spectra acquired through May 2020 and applies photometric normalisation to correct for illumination differences [3]. Orbital compositional context: SP was designed to measure the spectrum of the surface directly beneath the spacecraft and was part of the LISM suite with the Terrain Camera and Multiband Imager, so that topography, multi-band imagery and spectra could be combined [6].
article.operating_principle: Reflectance spectroscopy works because a surface absorbs some wavelengths more than others. An instrument receives sunlight reflected by the surface, separates it into wavelength bands, and divides the measured intensity by a reference (usually sunlight or a calibration target). The shape of the resulting curve, including the position, depth and width of absorption bands, is compared with laboratory spectra. For the VNIS: the instrument, mounted on the front of the rover at about 0.69 m above the ground and viewing at about 45 degrees, receives reflected sunlight [3][4]; AOTF elements select wavelength bands in a visible/near-infrared imaging channel and in a non-imaging shortwave-infrared spectrometer channel [3][4]; detectors record intensities at each band, and the channels acquire data simultaneously according to the search summary of the Chang'e-3 VNIS paper [1]. For SP: the spectrometer views the lunar surface below the spacecraft through a narrow field of view of 0.23 degrees [6]; two diffraction gratings disperse reflected light into 296 wavelengths covering the visible to near-infrared [6]; calibration is treated in Yamamoto et al. (2011), identified in a search summary but not accessed in this run [9].
article.scientific_importance: Spectral measurements at the surface are the ground truth that orbital mapping has to match. Spectra from a rover can test whether orbital spectral interpretations agree with the material actually at the surface, and can detect fine-grained or dusty material that a broad orbital pixel averages out. The Chang'e-4 VNIS far-side results are described in search metadata as the first in-situ far-side spectra [2] (not verified in the full text). Orbital point spectra from SP, combined with the Terrain Camera and Multiband Imager, form a multi-scale data set; SP's coverage complements the nine-band Multiband Imager on the same spacecraft [6][7]. Both examples have limited spatial coverage, so their main scientific value lies in calibrated, well-located spectra and in cross-calibration against other instruments rather than in mapping.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a visible and infrared spectrometer. Dispersing technology, spectral range, number of channels, field of view and whether the instrument images or measures a point all change mass, power and volume. Values below are tied to the named instrument and source. Where the sources reviewed do not provide a value it is recorded as 'not publicly specified in pages accessed' and set to null. The three examples are not directly comparable: two are rover-mounted instruments with an imaging channel and a point channel, and one is a non-imaging orbital spectrometer. Comparable-looking fields are shown in examples[] only for each instrument.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: The surface examples must tolerate lunar day and night temperature swings, dust and the need for a sunlit target during daytime operation. The VNIS includes a dust-proofing calibration unit according to a search summary of the Chang'e-3 paper [1]. Specific thermal, radiation and dust tolerance values are not publicly specified in pages accessed. The orbital SP example observes reflected sunlight from a moving spacecraft, so signal depends on solar illumination, viewing geometry and attitude/pointing accuracy; specific pointing and thermal requirements for SP are not publicly specified in pages accessed. Calibration is operationally important for both: the VNIS performs in-situ calibration [1], SP calibration is treated in Yamamoto et al. (2011) [9] (not accessed in this run), and photometric correction for illumination is required to compare spectra taken at different times or angles [3].
article.limitations: Point-like sampling: a point or small-footprint spectrometer measures one spot at a time, so a rover or orbiter must visit or revisit targets to build a dataset. Pointing dependence: narrow fields of view (0.23 degrees for SP; 8.5 and 3.6 degrees for the VNIS VNIR and SWIR channels) mean targeting errors can sample the wrong material [4][6]. Illumination dependence: reflectance depends on solar angle and viewing geometry, and corrections are required [3]. Dust and weathering: dust coverage can mask spectra; search metadata for a 2021 GRL study reports partial dust coverage on four rocks measured by the VNIS, but that paper was not accessed and is treated as unverified. Spectral-range overlap: the SP NIR1 and NIR2 ranges overlap the near-infrared band of other instruments (see payload 061, not yet written), so instrument choice is a trade-off between band count, footprint and platform.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: The VNIS is a rover-mounted instrument: the sources describe mounting on the front of the Yutu (Chang'e-3) and Yutu-2 (Chang'e-4) rovers at about 0.69 m, viewing at about 45 degrees [1][3][4]. The SP was installed on the SELENE (Kaguya) spacecraft together with the Terrain Camera and Multiband Imager, as shown in the JAXA figure [6]. No lander, rover or spacecraft compatibility is asserted beyond these descriptions.
transportation_process: Surface (VNIS): the instrument was part of each Chang'e mission's lander and rover stack. Earth integration, launch, lunar transfer and landing are not described in detail in the sources reviewed; interface evidence for the specific lander and rover configuration is not verified in this run.
Surface (VNIS): deployment is by rover mobility; the sources reviewed do not describe a separate deployment mechanism, but this is not explicitly stated.
Surface (VNIS): power, data and thermal interfaces are not publicly specified in pages accessed.

Orbiter (SP): installation on the SELENE spacecraft with TC and MI is shown in the JAXA figure [6]. Launch, cruise, orbit insertion and commissioning are part of the SELENE mission record and are not verified in detail in this run.

Orbiter (SP): SP pointing relies on spacecraft attitude control; the SP data interface is assumed to pass through the spacecraft data system, and neither the interface specification nor commissioning dates are verified in this run.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: VNIS: rover-mounted with a fixed mounting at about 0.69 m and a 45-degree viewing angle (secondary summaries) [1][3][4]. SP: fixed to the spacecraft, observing the surface below the spacecraft [6]. Neither example's deployment is verified beyond these descriptions.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Chang'e-3 (Yutu) and Chang'e-4 (Yutu-2) rover VNIS instruments; SELENE (Kaguya) LISM suite with the Spectral Profiler [1][3][6].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a named lander, rover or spacecraft is asserted beyond the rover mounting and spacecraft installation described in the sources. Interface evidence for any future lander or rover is not verified.

article.historical_significance: The Chang'e-3 and Chang'e-4 rover VNIS instruments are examples of in-situ visible/near-infrared spectroscopy on the lunar surface. The Chang'e-4 far-side spectra are reported as a possible view of mantle-derived material [2]; that interpretation is recorded from search metadata and was not verified against the full paper. The SELENE (Kaguya) Spectral Profiler formed part of a three-instrument imaging and spectral suite; its band count and wavelength coverage gave a spectral record of the lunar surface that complemented the Multiband Imager [6][7]. The current operating status of these instruments in later mission phases was not verified in this run.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: Primary-source gap for VNIS specifications: the SPIE primary paper [1] was not readable in this run; the Chang'e-3 spectral ranges come from a secondary summary and a review [10]; the spectral resolution (2-12 nm) comes from a secondary aggregator and is not verified. Chang'e-4 VNIS numbers (450-945 nm, 8.5 and 3.6 degree fields of view, 96 spectra) come from search excerpts of the Remote Sensing and ISPRS papers [3][4] and were not checked against full text. Mass, dimensions and power: no verified values were found for any of the three instruments. SP launch date (14 September 2007) comes from a search excerpt [7]. SP operating dates and data-release history were not established. Current mission status of the VNIS instruments and SP was not verified. Mineralogical interpretations (low-calcium pyroxene and olivine) come from search metadata for the 2019 Nature paper [2]. Yamamoto et al. (2011) [9] and the 2019 Sensors paper [5] were identified but not accessed (the MDPI page returned HTTP 403). Cross-reference conflict: payload 041 refers VNIS to payload 035 and describes the SWIR channel as single-point [11]; this article's characterisation differs and the catalogue owner should reconcile the pointers.

data_quality_notes: Chang'e-3 VNIS primary source (SPIE paper 92630D) returned no readable content; spectral ranges come from a secondary summary and a review, and spectral resolution (2-12 nm) from a secondary aggregator. Not verified.
Mass, dimensions and power are not verified for any of the three instruments. The approx. 2 W figure in a search fragment for the Chang'e-3 VNIS is unattributed and not used.
SELENE Spectral Profiler mass, power and dimensions are not stated on the JAXA page. A dimension-annotated LISM figure exists but cannot be assigned to SP with confidence.

Chang'e-4 VNIS figures (450-945 nm imaging channel, 8.5 and 3.6 degree fields of view, 96 spectra through May 2020, photometric normalisation) come from search excerpts of two papers not read in full.
The 2019 Nature paper (Li et al.) mineralogical interpretation and 'first in-situ far-side spectra' claim come from search metadata; the full text was not retrieved.
The Sensors 2019 paper on VNIS in-flight verification (MDPI, 19(12), 2806) returned HTTP 403 and was not accessed. Yamamoto et al. (2011) on SP calibration was identified but not accessed.

SP launch date (14 September 2007) is from a search excerpt of the 2008 MI objectives paper; the full text was not retrieved. The JAXA press release of 14 December 2007 was reached (HTTP 200) but its SP statements were seen only in a search excerpt.
SP operating dates, data-release history and current mission status are not established. The current status of the Chang'e-3 and Chang'e-4 VNIS in later mission phases is not verified.

Boundary conflict: payload 041 describes the VNIS SWIR channel as a single-point spectrometer and refers VNIS to payload 035. This article treats VNIS as a combined VNIR imaging and SWIR point instrument and treats VNIS as its primary home. The catalogue owner should reconcile payload 035 and 041 pointers.
Payload 061 (Near-infrared spectrometer) is not yet written; the NIR1/NIR2 boundary with 061 is described generally and should be revisited when 061 is generated.
No verified direct image assets were found for the Chang'e-3 or Chang'e-4 VNIS. The only verified images are two JAXA SELENE figures for the SP example and overview.
Transportation and deployment: no verified lander or rover interface evidence for either VNIS or SP; compatibility is not asserted. Images array for transportation is empty.
Mineralogical absorption-band statement (pyroxene and olivine features near 1 and 2 micrometres) is general spectroscopy knowledge and is not cited to a specific source in this run.
The Chang'e-3 VNIS dust-proofing calibration unit and in-situ calibration function come from a search summary of the SPIE paper, not the primary text.
